title: Process Models: Schramm, Berlo, Westley–MacLean, Newcomb

ctx-endless.prompt: Which statement about Schramm’s 1954 chapter is correct?
options: It rejects the Shannon–Weaver diagram and replaces it with a completely new drawing.
It adapts the radio-circuit-like chain to human communication and stresses that every participant both encodes and decodes and that the process has no clear ends.
It treats communication as an event specific to mass communication.
It never mentions feedback.
ctx-endless.explain: The second option is right: Schramm takes the engineering chain, uses it for humans and adds the ideas that everyone both encodes and decodes and that the process is endless. The first option is tempting because the story “the new model replaces the old” is easy to believe; but the chapter itself uses the old drawing as a starting point. The third option is wrong: the chapter describes the general process of communication before mass communication. The fourth option is wrong: feedback is defined separately in the chapter.

ctx-why.prompt: A city puts warning posters on its streets. Everyone notices the posters, but most older people do not understand a technical term in them. Where would you look for the problem in Schramm’s framework?
options: The poster was not printed large enough; the problem is the capacity of the channel.
The message arrived undistorted, but the readers’ circle of experience overlaps too little with the term; the problem is sought in the overlap of the two circles.
The problem is only the readers’ inattention; the model has no place for it.
There is no problem: by Lasswell’s formula the question “with what effect?” has already been answered.
ctx-why.explain: The second option is right: the message got through, but meaning is built in the receiver’s experience, and Schramm’s two circles show exactly that. The first option is tempting because “it did not get through” is the easiest diagnosis; but the poster was seen, and the problem is in understanding. The third option blames the receiver and thereby switches the model off, which is just what process models prevent. The fourth option treats the question “with what effect?” as answered instead of asked.

who-when.prompt: True or false: Westley and MacLean’s model starts from Newcomb’s ABX framework and was published before Berlo’s book.
who-when.explain: True. Westley and MacLean begin by describing the simple communication act with Newcomb’s A–B–X model and add to it a C role for mass communication; the article appeared in 1957 (its first version in 1955), Berlo’s book in 1960. The order can get muddled because textbooks arrange models by topic; the publication order is 1953, 1955–57, 1960.

claim-map.prompt: A student says, “communication is nothing more than whether the message reaches its destination.” What is the four process models’ common objection?
options: Reaching is not enough: meaning, the participants’ relationship and the return must be taken into account too.
The meaning of a message is determined only by the source’s intention.
The receiver is unimportant in communication; the channel determines everything.
Communication should be studied only at the face-to-face level.
claim-map.explain: The first option is right: what the four models have in common is that they redefine the success of transmission through the receiver, the relationship and the return. The second option is tempting because “the source’s intention” seems to fit Berlo’s stress on purpose; but Berlo, too, calls the receiver one of the most important links in the process. The third option turns the point upside down; the fourth contradicts Westley and MacLean’s effort to cover mass communication.

concepts-field.prompt: A doctor says to a patient, “the drug has contraindications”; the patient looks bewildered. According to Schramm’s model, which move makes communication easiest?
options: Repeating the sentence more loudly.
Recoding the same thing with signs close to the patient’s experience (an example, an analogy).
Stopping the patient from asking questions.
The doctor making no concessions from his professional language.
concepts-field.explain: The second option is right: the message lies outside the patient’s circle, and the remedy is to move the signs into the overlap of the two circles. The first option is tempting because reading the problem as “it was not heard” is easy (channel and noise logic); but the patient has heard and has not understood. The third option closes the question and cuts off feedback; the fourth fixes the overlap instead of enlarging it.

concepts-glossary.prompt: In Westley and MacLean’s terms: a television viewer tries a well-advertised detergent, and the purchase enters a market survey’s data. What is this?
options: Purposive feedback: the viewer deliberately answered the seller.
Non-purposive feedback: the viewer produced data even without meaning to give feedback.
A C role: the viewer became a gatekeeper.
X′: the viewer turned into an abstraction.
concepts-glossary.explain: The second option is right: Westley and MacLean give this very example; the purchase becomes data for a market survey without the viewer’s intention. The first option is tempting because “feedback = a deliberate answer” sounds plausible; but purposive feedback is what is deliberately sent back, like an angry reader’s letter to an editor. The third and fourth options confuse other concepts (C and X′).

assumptions-shared.prompt: True or false: according to Berlo, source and receiver are two independent functions and make up the beginning and end of communication.
assumptions-shared.explain: False. Berlo writes that the source seems to be the beginning and the receiver the end, but that this is only a cut we make in order to talk about the model; he says it is not meaningful to assume the two functions are independent. “Beginning and end” is the language of linear models; Berlo’s concept of process says the opposite.

how-schramm.prompt: A writer reads an article aloud before publishing it and corrects the repeated sentences. In Schramm’s terms, what is this?
options: Feedback from the receiver
Feedback from one’s own message
Removal of channel noise
Enlarging the circle of experience
how-schramm.explain: The second option is right: Schramm counts hearing our own voice and correcting a mispronunciation, or seeing what we have written and correcting a spelling mistake, as feedback from our own message. The first option is tempting because feedback is often taught as “a reaction coming from the other side”; but Schramm separates two kinds. The third option is wrong because the writer is not removing an outside disturbance; the fourth is wrong because the writer is not changing his own experience.

how-newcomb.prompt: A friend you like praises a documentary. In Newcomb’s framework (other things being equal), what is the most likely outcome?
options: Your view of the documentary moves closer to your friend’s.
Your view moves away from your friend’s.
Nothing happens; communication only carries information.
You cannot form a view without watching the documentary.
how-newcomb.explain: The first option is right: if B likes A, B’s perception of X moves toward A’s after the communication. The third option is tempting because it is the view of line models (communication = information transfer); Newcomb says the relationship also changes the view of X. The second option describes what may happen with someone you dislike and contradicts the condition “other things being equal”; the fourth is a claim outside A–B–X.

how-wm.prompt: According to Westley and MacLean, on whose behalf does a newspaper’s news editor (the C role) make choices?
options: On behalf of A, the source of the news: he passes on A’s message.
On behalf of the receiver B: he selects the Xs suited to B’s needs and problems.
Only on his own behalf: his selection has no relation to anyone.
On behalf of advertisers: the income comes from them.
how-wm.explain: The second option is right: in the article C is the person who selects as B’s agent; his survival depends on satisfying B’s needs. The first option is tempting because the habit of “news source = A” is strong; but C is defined precisely as not being a purposive A. The fourth option is an economic claim from outside the model and is not in the 1957 article; the third option cuts C off from B and is therefore wrong.

how-berlo.prompt: A salesman does not believe in the product he sells, and it shows. Which of Berlo’s factors explains this?
options: The source’s communication skills (writing and speaking)
The source’s attitude toward the subject matter
The sensory nature of the channel
The receiver’s knowledge level
how-berlo.explain: The second option is right: Berlo writes that the source’s attitude toward the subject matter leaks into his message and that a salesman cannot sell what he does not believe in. The first option is tempting because “he cannot speak persuasively” comes to mind; but the problem is belief, not skill. The third and fourth options are features of the channel and the receiver, not of the source.

how-lab.prompt: In the Mr. Biggott episode, which question does Schramm’s model make you ask?
options: Was the cartoon distorted in the channel?
How did the cartoon’s signs meet the reader’s experience and frame of reference?
How many people saw the cartoon?
Was the cartoonist’s encoder strong enough?
how-lab.explain: The second option is right: the problem is how the signs settled into the reader’s frame, and Schramm’s circles make you ask exactly that. The first option is tempting because the line model’s first reflex is to look for “distortion in the message”; but the cartoon arrived undistorted and the meaning went off the rails inside the reader. The third option measures reach and the fourth the strength of encoding; both miss the receiver’s active interpretation.

evidence-test.prompt: True or false: according to Schramm, a good communication model is one that copies exactly what goes on inside the black box.
evidence-test.explain: False. Schramm says most of communication takes place in the black box of the nervous system and that models are therefore analogies; the yardstick is whether a model lets you make predictions. The “copy” yardstick treats a model as a photograph instead of a map; Berlo, too, stresses that a map cannot draw the territory completely.

crit-myth.prompt: Which statement about the “process” emphasis in Berlo’s 1960 book is the most accurate?
options: Berlo draws communication as a circle and makes feedback the main box of the model.
Berlo argues that a process has no beginning, end or fixed order and that the elements affect one another; but the model in the book is a list of components.
Berlo says that communication is linear and that process is an illusion.
Berlo defines process through Shannon–Weaver’s concept of channel capacity.
crit-myth.explain: The second option is right: Berlo defines process as having no beginning or end and as an interaction of elements, and says a model freezes the process like a photograph; the model itself is a list of six components. The first option is tempting because the habit “process = circle” is strong; in the book feedback is not a box in the first model. The third option turns Berlo’s thesis upside down; the fourth confuses concepts.

crit-limits.prompt: A critic says, “the Westley–MacLean model does not show the owners’ interests in news-making.” Based on the text, which reply is the fairest?
options: The model has already solved all of these problems.
The model calls itself a paradigm, not a theory, and leaves the gap between C’s role prescription and behaviour open as an empirical question; but owners’ interests really do not appear in the model.
The criticism is meaningless because journalists are always neutral.
The model was designed only for face-to-face communication, so the criticism is off topic.
crit-limits.explain: The second option is right: it both concedes that the criticism touches a real gap and reports the model’s own framework (paradigm, the gap between role and behaviour) accurately. The first option exaggerates the model’s claim; the third contradicts the fact that Westley and MacLean themselves write that a reporter may act as an advocate; the fourth is wrong because the model was written precisely to cover mass communication.

today-digital.prompt: Your uncle posts news links to the family group every day. In Westley and MacLean’s distinction, what would make him an A instead of a C?
options: Posting a large number of links
Posting the links with the aim of changing the group’s perception of an issue
The links coming from newspaper sites
The group being large
today-digital.explain: The second option is right: in the article A is the person who transmits in order to change B’s view of an X; without intention the transmitted thing is an X, and the one who selects and passes it on is in the C role. The authors add that the distinction is made in role prescriptions and not in actual performance. The other options are criteria of quantity or of the type of source; the model does not look at these.

exam-patterns.prompt: An exam question: “This is the model that adds a gatekeeper role to Newcomb’s ABX model and adapts it to mass communication.” Which is the correct answer?
options: Lasswell’s model
Berlo’s SMCR model
The Westley–MacLean model
Schramm’s two-circle model
exam-patterns.explain: Westley and MacLean add C (the gatekeeper) to Newcomb’s ABX. Lasswell is a tempting wrong answer because the questions “who” and “through what channel” evoke mass communication; but the formula dates from 1948 and has no gatekeeper role. Berlo has a “channel” but no gatekeeper role; Schramm’s two circles describe meaning between persons.

summary.prompt: True or false: the names “circular model” and “field of experience” appear in Schramm’s 1954 chapter.
summary.explain: False (according to the scanned text). In the chapter the two circles are described as “accumulated experience” and the process as an “endless current”; in 1971 the words are “frame of reference”. “Circular model” and “field of experience” are common textbook labels; use them in an exam, but know the source text’s own words too.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the factors Berlo lists for the source-encoder?
options: Communication skills
Attitudes
Knowledge level
Gatekeeping
quiz.explain: Gatekeeping belongs to Westley and MacLean’s C role and is not a source factor in Berlo. Berlo’s list is communication skills, attitudes, knowledge level and social-cultural system. The mix-up arises because both models use the words “channel” and “source” and both come after Lasswell.

quiz.prompt: True or false: in Schramm’s 1954 chapter the overlap of the two circles stands for the shared part of the two participants’ accumulated experience; the larger the overlap, the easier the communication.
quiz.explain: True. Schramm links a large overlap of the circles with easy communication, a small overlap with difficult communication and no overlap with impossibility. The yardstick is the overlap of experience, not “intelligence” or “education” level; that is a common misreading.

quiz.prompt: Match each model with its main contribution.
pairs: The overlap of two people’s circles of experience
The strain toward symmetry among A, B and X
The gatekeeper C and three feedback lines
Lists of factors in source, message, channel and receiver
quiz.explain: Schramm’s signature is the two circles; Newcomb’s is the triangle of A, B and X; Westley–MacLean’s is the C and the feedback lines added to Newcomb’s triangle; Berlo’s is the lists of factors inside the components. The pair most often mixed up is Newcomb and Westley–MacLean: the second builds on the first, but C and mass communication are only in the second.

quiz.prompt: Put the events in chronological order (oldest to newest).
items: Newcomb’s paper “An Approach to the Study of Communicative Acts” (1953)
Westley and MacLean’s Journalism Quarterly article (1957)
Berlo’s book The Process of Communication (1960)
quiz.explain: The order: 1953 Newcomb, 1954 Schramm, 1955 the first version of Westley–MacLean, 1957 the revised version, 1960 Berlo, 1971 Schramm’s rewrite. The most common mistake is to take the year Schramm wrote the chapter (1952) for its publication year; another is to forget that Westley–MacLean had a version before 1957.

quiz.prompt: Place the roles in the Westley–MacLean model.
quiz.text: In Westley and MacLean’s model A stands for {{1}} roles, B for {{2}} roles and C for {{3}} roles.

options: advocacy (purposive transmitter)
behavioural system (receiver)
channel (gatekeeper)
channel (gatekeeper)
advocacy (purposive transmitter)
behavioural system (receiver)
behavioural system (receiver)
channel (gatekeeper)
advocacy (purposive transmitter)

quiz.explain: A is the advocacy roles: it transmits purposively. B is the behavioural system roles: the receiver, that is a person, group or society. C is the channel roles: it selects and transmits non-purposively on the receiver’s behalf; it is the gatekeeper. The commonest mistake is to take C for an intermediary of A; in the article C is B’s agent.

quiz.scenario: The editor of a local news site picks three items out of the dozens discussed in the city council and writes them up for readers. Readers keep writing comments; looking at them, the editor adjusts which topics to stress the next day. In the article the editor avoids the council’s technical terms. (Hypothetical scenario.)

parts.prompt: What is the editor’s role in the Westley–MacLean model?
options: A (advocate)
B (behavioural system)
C (channel, gatekeeper)
parts.explain: The editor selects from council topics the readers cannot reach and passes them on: C. The council members (as purposive transmitters) are A; the readers are B. Even if the editor is a committed advocate, the article treats that as a gap between role prescription and behaviour.

parts.prompt: Along which line do the readers’ comments run?
options: Feedback from B to C
Feedback from C to A
A message from A to B
parts.explain: The reader (B) sends the comment to the editor (C): feedback from B to C. The line from C to A is the information the editor returns to the council; A to B is the direction of the message. If writing a comment is deliberate, it is purposive feedback.

parts.prompt: On which of Schramm’s ideas does the editor’s avoidance of technical terms rest?
options: The endlessness of the process
Enlarging the overlap of the circles of experience
Getting feedback from one’s own message
parts.explain: Choosing signs close to the readers’ experience enlarges the overlap of the two circles. The endlessness of the process is a more general observation; feedback from one’s own message concerns the editor reading and correcting his own text.

quiz.takeaway: The same newsroom can be read with two models: Westley–MacLean maps the roles and the feedback lines; Schramm makes you ask how well the chosen language fits the readers’ experience.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the name “Osgood–Schramm circular model” is correct?
options: The name itself appears explicitly in Schramm’s 1954 chapter.
In his chapter Schramm says in a footnote that he owes a psychology diagram to Osgood; the combined name is a common label in textbooks.
Osgood published this model after Schramm and cited him.
The model is Shannon and Weaver’s original diagram.
quiz.explain: The second option is right: in 1954 Schramm thanks Osgood in a footnote, and in 1971 he attributes to Osgood the scheme that adds the interpreter role; the name “Osgood–Schramm circular model” is common in secondary sources and does not occur in that combined form in the two Schramm texts scanned. The first option is tempting because the label is so entrenched in books that it is assumed to be in the source text. The third and fourth options confuse the chronology and the identity of the model.

quiz.prompt: According to Pooley, what job did Schramm’s “four founders” story do for the field?
options: It documented the true list of the field’s founders once and for all.
It gave a field that was growing institutionally but weak in standing a past and a legitimacy borrowed from high-status pioneers.
It redefined the field as a branch of economics.
It completely rejected the history of process models.
quiz.explain: The second option is right: according to Pooley the field had a legitimacy deficit and Schramm closed it by writing a “founding fathers” story about four names. The first option is tempting because textbooks report the list as fact; Pooley treats it as a choice of narrative. The third and fourth options are not in the text.

quiz.prompt: True or false: according to Westley and MacLean, feedback in mass communication is generally minimised or delayed compared with face-to-face communication.
quiz.explain: True. The article names two things that separate mass communication from face-to-face communication: fewer sense modalities, and “orientative” feedback that is minimised or delayed. The confusion comes from feedback being fast on modern platforms; but that is not the claim of the 1957 article.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is one of Sapienza and colleagues’ (2016) main arguments about the transmission model?
options: The transmission metaphor was born only with Shannon and Weaver.
The roots of the transmission metaphor go back before Shannon and Weaver, to telegraph terms and general semantics; Shannon used “transmission” literally.
The concept of feedback first appeared with process models.
The transmission model has never existed historically.
quiz.explain: The second option is right: the article argues that the transmission metaphor came from sources before Shannon and Weaver, such as Hartley, Nyquist and general semantics, and that Shannon used “transmission” literally. The first option is the view the article disputes. The third option is tempting because feedback is so often linked with process models; the article writes that the concept comes from cybernetics. The fourth option is not the article’s thesis.
